drafts.title: Fire Prevention Week: where your family charges stuff matters
drafts.window: Thu ~10 AM MT today (soft Thursday slot, keeps 6 PM for F1). Fri 11 AM MT at the latest, before the week ends Saturday.
drafts.angle: A plain, calm, two-minute safety check for every house with phones, e-bikes and an EV charger. The EV is not the scary part; the phone on the bed is. Timely because the week ends Saturday.
bullets: Fire Prevention Week is Oct 4-10, 2026. NFPA's theme: "Charge into Fire Safety: Safe Charging Is a Superpower."
Use the charger that came with the device or one the maker approves. Buy products listed by UL, ETL or CSA.
Charge on a hard, flat surface, not beds, couches or under pillows. Unplug when full.
Charge big batteries like e-bikes, scooters and power tools outside when possible, and never block exits.
Stop using anything that gets very hot, swells, smells odd, leaks, smokes, or pops or hisses.
drafts.body:
$0 and two minutes.

That is all it takes to walk your house tonight and check where everybody charges their stuff.

This is Fire Prevention Week, and this year the fire folks are talking about charging. Not because EVs are scary. Because of the phone on the pillow and the cheap e-bike charger in the hallway.

Here is the list, plain and simple:
Use the charger that came with it, or one the maker approves.
Look for UL, ETL or CSA on the label.
Hard, flat surface. Not the bed, not the couch, not under a pillow.
Unplug when it is full.
E-bikes, scooters and big tool batteries, charge them outside if you can, and never where they block a door.
If anything gets really hot, swells up, smells funny or starts hissing, stop using it.

My car charges in the garage on [my setup ___]. Honestly the thing I checked first was [the grandkids' phones / my e-bike / the power strip behind the TV ___].

Where do your grandkids charge their phones at your house?
drafts.shortForm: $0 and two minutes. That's all it takes to check where your family charges stuff tonight. Fire Prevention Week tips: maker's charger, hard surface, never on the bed, unplug when full, e-bikes outside. [photo: my garage charger setup ___] Where do your grandkids charge their phones?
drafts.ocrNote: Strong. Family safety, his own garage photo, easy save and repost, ends with a grandparent question. Keep it calm and useful, not a fear post.
drafts.pixelPrompt: 15 seconds in the garage: "This is where my car charges. And this [phone on the nightstand / e-bike] is the one I actually worry about. Here's the fix."

drafts.title: 0.3%: the robot-takeover number nobody is sharing
drafts.window: Fri 1 PM MT (best slot this week for a talker). Backup Thu ~6:30 PM MT if F1 waits.
drafts.angle: The scary "81% of jobs" headline went around last night. The same study says robots are cheaper than people for only 0.3% of work today. Calm, honest, not dismissive. Exactly the "make AI less scary" lane.
bullets: Robots can technically do about 74% of physical job tasks, mostly in tightly controlled settings. Add AI chatbots and about 81% of tasks are "exposed."
But robots are cost-competitive for just 0.3% of job tasks today. At past price drops (about 3% a year), reaching 10% would take around 40 years.

Closest case: packers, about $45,000 a year for the robot vs about $49,000 for the worker. Welding robots cost about 5 times more. Dishwashers and janitors: robots are still several times more expensive.
Honest caveat: about 300,000 workers already have jobs where robots can do 95% of the tasks, and the authors say the 40 years could shrink if prices fall faster.
drafts.body:
0.3 percent.

You probably saw the scary number going around last night. "81% of jobs exposed to AI and robots." That came from a real study by one of the big AI companies.

Here is the half of that same study nobody is sharing. Robots are actually cheaper than a person for about 0.3 percent of the work Americans do today. Not 81. Point three.

The closest job is packing boxes. A robot runs about $45,000 a year. The worker makes about $49,000. That is close. Welding? The robot costs about five times more. Washing dishes, cleaning buildings? Still several times more expensive than a person.

At the rate robot prices have been dropping, the study says it would take around 40 years to get to even 10 percent.

I am not going to tell you nobody loses a job. About 300,000 people already do work a robot could mostly handle, and prices could fall faster. But "can do" and "makes sense to buy" are two very different things.

[what I tell my kids / grandkids about this ___]

Does that number make you feel better or worse about AI?
drafts.shortForm: 0.3%. That's how much of America's work a robot actually does cheaper than a person today. That's from the AI company's own study. The closest job, packing boxes: about $45,000 a year for the robot vs $49,000 for the worker. Does that make you feel better or worse about AI?
drafts.ocrNote: Strong. Number opener, myth-buster in plain words, fits the "make AI less scary" push, invites replies from both sides. Stick to the study's numbers; do not promise nobody loses work.
drafts.pixelPrompt: 20 seconds: "Everybody's scared robots are coming for our jobs. Here's the number from the AI company itself: point three percent. Here's what that means for [my kids / my grandkids]: ___."
drafts.replyTarget: Quote the "81%" post from @Polymarket (https://x.com/Polymarket/status/2107977145956135026) with one line: "Here's the other half of that study."

drafts.title: Medicare open enrollment starts Oct 15: let AI read the boring letter, not the stranger on the phone
drafts.window: Fri ~11:30 AM MT, or Mon ~1 PM MT (Monday's hottest slot, right before Oct 15).
drafts.angle: The yearly "your plan is changing" letter is long and confusing. AI can put it in plain English for free. But the real plan comparison and sign-up go through Medicare.gov, because scammers are buying the top search ads. Not a twin of the Sep 30 MyChart post.
bullets: Medicare Open Enrollment runs Oct 15 to Dec 7, 2026. Changes start Jan 1, 2027.
Your plan's "Annual Notice of Change" letter lists how 2027 costs and benefits change. Compare plans at Medicare.gov/plan-compare or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).
FTC (Sep 28): scammers pay to show up at the top of search results with look-alike sites. Type Medicare.gov directly and look for .gov.
Free one-on-one help: your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP).

drafts.title: 85,774 garages just acted like one power plant
drafts.window: Fri ~11 AM MT (start of the Friday block), or Thu ~6:30 PM MT if F1 holds for the actual departure.
drafts.angle: Regular California homeowners got paid to help their neighbors keep the lights on at dinnertime. Keep it about families and a check in the mail, not megawatts. Different from your Powershare post: this is home batteries helping the grid, not the car powering the house. Quote-post of a watched account (Sawyer Merritt).
bullets: Tuesday evening, Oct 6, 85,774 California homes with Tesla Powerwalls sent 601 MW to the grid at peak demand. The whole Powerwall fleet peaked at a record 634 MW.
Participating batteries delivered 932 MWh over the event (Tesla VPP dashboard, per Drive Tesla).
Tesla says Powerwall owners in these California programs earn incentives for the energy they send back. Tesla does not publish a per-home payout, so no dollar figure.
Sawyer Merritt's post on it: 3,400+ likes, 117K views at pack time.
drafts.body:
85,774 homes.

That is how many California families just did the job of one big power plant. Tuesday at dinnertime, when everybody gets home and turns on the stove and the AC, their home batteries kicked in and sent power back to the grid. Enough to cover about 601 megawatts at the peak.

Nobody built a new plant. Nobody's lights went out. And the owners get paid for the power they sent back.

That is the part I like. The battery in your garage is not just for when the power goes out. It can earn its keep on a normal Tuesday.

[would I sign up if Xcel offered something like this here in Grand Junction: ___]

Would you let your battery help the neighbors for a check?

(Do not claim Xcel has a program like this unless you have checked.)

drafts.ocrNote: OK. Big verified quote target and a pocketbook question, but no dollar opener (no per-home payout published) and battery is a soft lane. Short quote form beats the long body here.
